title: de Broglie Matter Waves & the Einstein–Planck Synthesis
topicTitle: Elementary idea of quantum mechanical model: de Broglie's wave equation
notes: **Einstein–Planck synthesis:** combining Einstein's mass–energy equivalence E = mc² with Planck's quantum relation E = hν gives mc² = hν, linking a particle's mass to a wave frequency.

**de Broglie wavelength:** since ν = c/λ, the relation becomes mc = h/λ, so the wavelength of a moving particle is λ = h/(mv) = h/p, where p = mv is the momentum. This is the de Broglie relation (1924).

**de Broglie wavelength for an electron:** for an electron accelerated through potential V, KE = eV = p²/2m, so p = √(2meV). Therefore λ = h/√(2meV). For V = 100 V, λ ≈ 0.123 nm, comparable to X-ray wavelengths.
**Inverse mass dependence:** λ ∝ 1/m — heavier objects have extremely short wavelengths, which is why macroscopic objects show no observable wave behaviour.

**Macro-object wave negligibility:** for a 1 kg ball moving at 1 m/s, λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ m, far smaller than any measurable scale (~10⁻¹⁵ m), so wave effects are undetectable and classical mechanics applies.

**Bohr quantization deduced via waves:** if an electron is a standing wave, only orbits whose circumference is an integer multiple of the wavelength (2πr = nλ) are stable — this naturally reproduces Bohr's quantization of angular momentum (mvr = nh/2π).

**Experimental confirmation:** Davisson and Germer (1927) observed diffraction of electrons by a nickel crystal, confirming the wave nature of electrons. G.P. Thomson independently confirmed it using electron transmission through thin gold foils.

**Electron diffraction patterns:** when electrons pass through a crystalline material, they produce ring diffraction patterns identical to X-ray diffraction, proving that electrons behave as waves with wavelength given by the de Broglie relation.

**Heisenberg (1927) introduction:** the wave picture of the electron led Heisenberg to the uncertainty principle, which states that position and momentum cannot both be known precisely at the same time.

**Wave–particle duality:** de Broglie's hypothesis established that ALL matter exhibits both wave and particle properties. The wave nature dominates at atomic scales; the particle nature dominates at macroscopic scales.

**Phase velocity vs group velocity:** the phase velocity of a de Broglie wave (v_p = E/p) exceeds the speed of light, which does not violate relativity because information is carried by the group velocity (v_g = dE/dp), which is always less than c.

**de Broglie relation for photons:** photons have zero rest mass but carry momentum p = E/c = h/λ. This is consistent with the de Broglie relation λ = h/p, establishing the universality of wave–particle duality.

**Thermal de Broglie wavelength:** at temperature T, a particle has average kinetic energy (3/2)kT, giving λ = h/√(3mkT). At room temperature, this is ~0.1 nm for electrons but ~10⁻¹¹ m for atoms — explaining why electron diffraction is observable but neutron diffraction requires crystals.

**Matter wave packet:** a real particle is not a pure plane wave (which would be infinitely extended) but a wave packet — a superposition of waves with slightly different wavelengths that is localised in space.
confusion: The de Broglie wavelength is NOT the physical size of the particle. It is the wavelength of the associated probability wave. A 0.1 nm electron wavelength does not mean the electron is 0.1 nm across.
de Broglie's relation applies to ALL matter, not just electrons. However, the effect is only observable for particles with atomic-scale masses because λ is inversely proportional to mass.

Wave–particle duality does NOT mean the electron is sometimes a wave and sometimes a particle. It is always a quantum object that exhibits wave-like or particle-like behaviour depending on the experimental setup.
The de Broglie wavelength changes with velocity. A fast electron has a shorter wavelength than a slow electron — this is why high-energy electron microscopes achieve better resolution.
practice: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at 2.19 × 10⁶ m/s (the velocity of an electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen). Solution: λ = h/mv = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴)/(9.109 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.19 × 10⁶) = 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁹ m = 0.332 nm. This equals the circumference of the first Bohr orbit divided by 2π, confirming 2πr = λ.

Find the de Broglie wavelength of a 150 g ball moving at 30 m/s. Solution: λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴/(0.150 × 30) = 1.47 × 10⁻³⁴ m. This is far too small to detect, explaining why we never see wave behaviour of everyday objects.

An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 200 V. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength. Solution: λ = h/√(2meV) = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴/√(2 × 9.109 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 200) = 8.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ m = 0.0868 nm (X-ray range).

Show that the de Broglie relation reproduces Bohr's quantization condition. Solution: From λ = h/p and 2πr = nλ: 2πr = nh/p = nh/mvr, giving mvr = nh/2π, which is Bohr's quantization of angular momentum.

Compare the de Broglie wavelengths of an electron and a proton moving at the same speed. Solution: λ_e/λ_p = m_p/m_e ≈ 1836. The proton's wavelength is ~1836 times shorter, which is why proton diffraction requires much higher energies to observe.
universalFacts: Louis de Broglie proposed matter waves in his 1924 PhD thesis. The examining committee was so uncertain about the idea that they sent it to Einstein for evaluation — Einstein endorsed it, and de Broglie was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1929.

Electron microscopes exploit the short de Broglie wavelength of high-energy electrons to achieve resolution far beyond optical microscopes. A 100 keV electron has λ ≈ 0.0037 nm, about 100,000 times shorter than visible light.

The concept of wave–particle duality was a cornerstone of quantum mechanics. Feynman called it 'a phenomenon which is impossible to explain in any classical way, and which has in it the heart of quantum mechanics.'

Davisson and Germer's 1927 electron diffraction experiment was initially accidental — a vacuum leak caused nickel oxide to reduce to crystalline nickel, and the unexpected diffraction pattern revealed the wave nature of electrons.

Neutron diffraction is now a standard technique in materials science. Thermal neutrons (λ ≈ 0.1 nm) diffract from crystal lattices similarly to X-rays, but neutrons interact with nuclear spins, making them ideal for studying magnetic materials.
